tool-use.q: Who runs the tool, the model or my code?
tool-use.a: Your code. For tools you define, Claude replies with stop_reason "tool_use" and a tool_use block naming the tool and its inputs. Your code runs it and sends the result back in a tool_result block in a new request, and only then can Claude use the result in its answer.

sources.title: Claude Platform docs: Tool use with Claude

tool-use.q: Does the model remember my earlier requests?
tool-use.a: No. The Messages API is stateless: you always send the full conversation history with each request. Anything the model should “remember”, including earlier tool calls and results, has to be in what your code sends.

sources.title: Claude Platform docs: Using the Messages API

agent-loop-limits.q: Why put the step limit in code instead of in the prompt?
agent-loop-limits.a: Because code runs the loop. Anthropic's guide says it's common to add stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations, “to maintain control”. A limit written only in the prompt depends on the model following it; a limit in the loop holds whatever the model does.

agent-loop-limits.q: Should tool errors be shown to the model?
agent-loop-limits.a: Yes, as the tool's result. Anthropic's guide says agents need “ground truth” from the environment at each step, such as tool call results, to judge their progress. An error is ground truth: with it, the model can try something else or report the problem; without it, it's guessing.

agent-guardrails.a: Instructions hidden in content the model reads from outside, such as a web page, a file or an email that a tool returns. OWASP's LLM01 describes it as happening when an LLM accepts input from external sources. The model may treat that text as instructions instead of data.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM01 Prompt Injection

agent-guardrails.q: Can a system prompt alone stop prompt injection?
agent-guardrails.a: Not reliably. OWASP lists clear instructions in the system prompt as one mitigation, but also says that it's unclear whether there are fool-proof ways to prevent prompt injection. So add guardrails that hold even when the model is fooled: least privilege, and human approval for high-risk actions.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM01 Prompt Injection

agent-guardrails.q: Which guardrails still work if the model is fooled?
agent-guardrails.a: The ones enforced outside the model. OWASP recommends least privilege (only the tools and permissions the task needs, handled in code) and human approval for high-risk actions. A tool the agent doesn't have can't be misused, and an action waiting for approval can't happen on its own.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM01 Prompt Injection
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM06 Excessive Agency

agent-evals.q: Should a grader check what the agent said, or what it did?
agent-evals.a: What it did. Anthropic's evals guide defines the outcome as the final state of the environment at the end of a trial: a booking agent may say “Your flight has been booked”, but the outcome is whether a reservation exists in the database. Graders that only read the transcript can pass false claims.

sources.title: Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents

agent-evals.q: What pass rate should a regression eval have?
agent-evals.a: Nearly 100%. Anthropic's guide says regression evals ask whether the agent still handles everything it used to, so they should almost always pass; a drop means a change broke something. Capability evals are different: they should start with a low pass rate, giving a hill to climb.

sources.title: Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents
